sections.title: The Nine Measurements
sections.tabSummary: What each output tells you about handling behavior
body: PFT Powder Flow Tester measurement outputs: what each number tells you about handling behavior.

A single flow function number doesn't tell a hopper designer everything they need. PFT's testing produces nine distinct outputs, each answering a different practical question about how a powder will actually behave in equipment.

Bulk density, measured at fill and final states, establishes the baseline the rest of the data builds from. Wall friction predicts how the powder interacts with the specific material a hopper or chute is built from, not a generic assumption. Flow index summarizes overall flowability. Arching dimensions and rat-hole diameter predict the two most common hopper discharge failures before either happens on the production line. Hopper half angle informs the actual geometry a new hopper needs. Carr Index and Hausner Ratio flag compressibility and caking risk. Time consolidation testing, run alongside the full flow function data, captures how flow behavior changes after a powder has sat in storage, a condition standard single-point testing misses entirely.

rows: How dense is the powder, loose and settled?
Will it stick to the hopper wall?
How well does it flow overall?
Will it arch and stop flowing?
Will it rat-hole through the center?
Is it prone to caking or poor compressibility?
Does flow behavior change after storage?

paragraphs: A flow function test that takes hours arrives too late to shape a formulation decision. It becomes a confirmation exercise after the powder is already committed to a process, not a design input.

PFT completes a full flow function test in 25 minutes. That speed is what makes powder flow characterization a genuine part of formulation work, tested and iterated on, rather than a final check run once at the end. For QA/QC, a separate faster test path exists specifically so routine quality checks don't require the full 25-minute battery every time.
